title: Making Cycle Reflectors Easier to See
transcript:
Thanks for looking over our project plan. We want to find out whether putting a reflector on a cyclist's ankle makes the cyclist easier to see at dusk. We found studies of bike-mounted reflectors.
That's a workable question. Be clear about why you picked the ankle. A reflector on the bag might be brighter, but an observer may recognise a cyclist by the pattern of movement rather than brightness alone.
Right. We can use the university's closed practice track so that we don't have to bring cars onto a public road. I thought we'd ask volunteers to stand by the fence and tell us when they spot someone.
Have them sit in a stationary car instead. The windscreen and the driver's position will affect what they see. You can leave the engine off and keep the headlights on at the same setting.
In that case we'll need a simple way for volunteers to register what they see. We could put numbered markers beside the track and have them call out the number they see the rider passing.
It'll be more reliable if they press a button. A camera can record the location of the rider at that point. Ask for a press when they can identify a cyclist, not as soon as they see any light.
Should everyone see the ankle reflector first and then the one on the bag? That would be simplest for the rider. We could finish a set before changing it.
Vary the order across volunteers. Once someone knows exactly where to look, they may respond faster the second time, regardless of which reflector they see. You need to make that advantage roughly equal between the two conditions.
I see. We're also likely to lose some light during the session. Would it make sense to run both trials for one volunteer before moving on to the next, instead of testing everybody on one condition at a time?
Yes, pair the trials fairly close together and record light levels anyway. For the final report, though, remember that seeing a cyclist on your empty track is quite different from seeing one on a busy street.
We'll say that other lights and traffic could change the result. Is there anything else you'd want us to include in the presentation?
Show the spread of individual responses as well as the averages. If the two averages are different but the results overlap a lot, that is worth explaining.

questions.prompt: The university owns the closed practice ____ used for the trial.
questions.explanation: 学生提出在大学封闭的练习车道上骑行，免去占用公共道路。

questions.prompt: Volunteers will observe from a stationary ____.
questions.explanation: 导师建议让志愿者坐在静止的汽车里，保留挡风玻璃和驾驶位置的影响。

questions.prompt: To signal that they can identify a cyclist, volunteers will press a ____.
questions.explanation: 导师建议志愿者在辨认出骑车人时按下按钮，由摄像机记录对应的位置。

questions.prompt: Why does the tutor recommend varying the order of the trials?
options: To avoid asking the rider to wear one reflector for too long.
To spread the advantage of knowing where to look across both conditions.
To give the camera enough time to adjust between trials.
questions.answer: To spread the advantage of knowing where to look across both conditions.
questions.explanation: 第二次尝试时，志愿者已经知道该往哪里看，变换顺序可以平衡这种熟悉优势。

questions.prompt: What should the students show in their presentation alongside the averages?
options: Recordings of traffic around the track.
A comparison of two different cameras.
questions.explanation: 导师提醒学生展示个体反应的分布，便于说明两组结果有多少重叠。
